On lattice-polarized K3 surfaces

Valery Alexeev Email address: valery@uga.edu Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Georgia, Athens, GA 30602, USA and Philip Engel Email address: pengel@uic.edu Address: Department of Mathematics, Statistics, and Computer Science, University of Illinois in Chicago, Chicago, IL 60607, USA
Date: November 3, 2025
Abstract.

We propose modifications to the commonly used definitions of lattice-polarized and lattice-quasipolarized smooth K3 surfaces, collecting various versions of the definition, and determining the effects of these choices on the resulting moduli space. We fill a gap in the theory, by replacing Weyl chambers with the new notion of a “small cone”: the true datum in the definition of lattice quasipolarized K3 surfaces. In addition, we describe the separated moduli stack and moduli space for lattice-polarized K3 surfaces with A​D​EADE singularities, an important notion for applications.

1. Introduction

Lattice polarizations on K3 surfaces, generalizing ordinary polarizations, were introduced and studied in an influential 1996 paper [Dol96] by Dolgachev. Unfortunately, Theorem 3.1 describing the fibers of the period map for lattice quasipolarized K3 surfaces in ibid. is incorrect with the given definitions, and this misconception has persisted throughout the literature to this day. In this paper, we give the corrected definition (Definition 4.2), for lattice-quasipolarized K3 surfaces for which [Dol96, Theorem 3.1] remains true (Theorem 4.7).

The difference between our definition and that of [Dol96] is explained in Remark 4.3. The two definitions agree over a Zariski open subset of the period space, and their difference only becomes apparent at non-separated points of moduli, where the fiber of the period map jumps.

In [Dol96], only smooth K3 surfaces are considered. In Section 5, we define lattice-polarized K3 surfaces with ADE singularities (Definitions 5.1 and 5.8).

Furthermore, we describe the precise structure of the stacks both of the lattice-quasipolarized smooth K3 surfaces (Theorem 4.22) and of the lattice-polarized A​D​EADE K3 surfaces (Theorem 5.5 and Corollary 5.10). Unlike the former, the latter stack is separated. The coarse moduli space of K3 surfaces with A​D​EADE singularities is separated as well. This is the version of the moduli space that is useful for many applications, for example it was used in [AE23]. The (generalized) small cones introduced in Definitions 4.9 and 5.6 are essential for this version of the moduli space.

We expect that our definition of lattice (quasi)polarization and the description of the stacks can be generalized to the setting of moduli of KK-trivial varieties, especially hyperkähler varieties.

This material was included in [AE21], an arXiv version of [AE23], but not in the condensed, published version. We have decided to make it widely available as a separate paper, to both clarify the problem and provide a solution to it.

Throughout the paper, we work over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}.

2. Smooth vs ADE K3 surfaces

Definition 2.1.

A K3 surface XX is a compact, complex, smooth surface which has a trivial canonical bundle 𝒪⁡(KX)≃𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}(K_{X})\simeq\mathcal{O}_{X} and irregularity zero, i.e. h1​(X,𝒪X)=0h^{1}(X,{\mathcal{O}}_{X})=0.

Any complex K3 surface is Kähler [Siu83] and any K3 surface admitting a line bundle LL with L2>0L^{2}>0 is algebraic and projective. When speaking of moduli of K3 surfaces, one is always faced with a choice: to work with smooth surfaces or with surfaces that can possibly have ADE (i.e. Du Val, or ordinary double point) singularities. Both options have their advantages:

(1) Smooth K3 surfaces are all diffeomorphic and share the same cohomology ring. The price that one pays is that instead of working with a polarization, i.e. an ample line bundle LL, one is forced to work with a quasipolarization, which is big, nef and semiample but whose intersection may be zero with finitely many smooth rational (−2)(-2)-curves on XX. An unfortunate issue is that the moduli stacks and coarse moduli spaces of smooth quasipolarized K3 surfaces are not separated.

(2) In contrast, when working with ADE K3 surfaces, one can work directly with polarized pairs (X¯,L¯)({\overline{X}},{\overline{L}}), where L¯{\overline{L}} is an ample line bundle. The moduli stacks and moduli spaces of polarized ADE surfaces are separated, at the cost of working with singular varieties. In other words, the filling (𝒳¯,ℒ¯)→(C,0)(\overline{{\mathcal{X}}},\overline{{\mathcal{L}}})\to(C,0) of a family of polarized ADE K3 surfaces (𝒳¯∗,ℒ¯∗)→C∗(\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\,\!^{*},\overline{{\mathcal{L}}}\,\!^{*})\to C^{*} over a punctured curve is unique, if it exists. Furthermore, the moduli stack is smooth, since deformations of ADE K3 surfaces are unobstructed by [BW74].

For any individual polarized ADE surface (X¯,L¯)({\overline{X}},{\overline{L}}), the corresponding smooth surface XX is the minimal resolution of singularities π:X→X¯\pi\colon X\to{\overline{X}}, and L=π∗​(L¯)L=\pi^{*}({\overline{L}}). Vice versa, for a smooth quasipolarized surface (X,L)(X,L), the line bundle LL is semiample and defines a contraction π:X→X¯\pi\colon X\to{\overline{X}} to its ADE companion, with L¯=π∗​(L){\overline{L}}=\pi_{*}(L). So, the pairs (X,L)(X,L) and (X¯,L¯)({\overline{X}},{\overline{L}}) are in a natural bijection.

Only when working with families does the difference become apparent, as was already noted in [BR75]. If f:(𝒳,ℒ)→(C,0)f\colon({\mathcal{X}},{\mathcal{L}})\to(C,0) is a family of smooth K3 surfaces for which the line bundle ℒt{\mathcal{L}}_{t} is ample for a generic fiber 𝒳t{\mathcal{X}}_{t} but ℒ0{\mathcal{L}}_{0} is not ample on 𝒳0{\mathcal{X}}_{0}, then one can replace ff by a non-isomorphic family f+:(𝒳+,ℒ+)→(C,0)f^{+}\colon({\mathcal{X}}^{+},{\mathcal{L}}^{+})\to(C,0) obtained from 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} by a flop in a (−2)(-2)-curve contained in the central fiber 𝒳0{\mathcal{X}}_{0}. Fiberwise, the two families are isomorphic, but not globally. As a consequence, the moduli functor and the coarse moduli space of smooth quasipolarized K3 surfaces are not separated.

However, the corresponding family f¯:𝒳¯→(C,0)\bar{f}\colon\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\to(C,0) of ADE surfaces does not exhibit this behavior. The extension over 00 is unique: It is obtained from 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}, resp. 𝒳+{\mathcal{X}}^{+}, by a contraction over CC defined by the semiample line bundle ℒ{\mathcal{L}}, resp. ℒ+{\mathcal{L}}^{+}.

By [Bri71], a filling (𝒳¯,ℒ¯)→(C,0)(\overline{{\mathcal{X}}},\overline{{\mathcal{L}}})\to(C,0) of a family of polarized ADE K3 surfaces (𝒳¯∗,ℒ¯∗)→C∗(\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\,\!^{*},\overline{{\mathcal{L}}}\,\!^{*})\to C^{*} admits, after a cyclic base change (C′,0)→(C,0)(C^{\prime},0)\to(C,0), a simultaneous crepant resolution (𝒳,ℒ)→(C′,0)({\mathcal{X}},{\mathcal{L}})\to(C^{\prime},0) with ℒ{\mathcal{L}} relatively semiample. The birational isomorphism φ¯:𝒳¯⇢𝒳¯+\overline{\varphi}\colon\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\dashrightarrow\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\,\!^{+} between two such fillings extending id𝒳¯∗{\rm id}_{\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\,\!^{*}} induces then a birational isomorphism on the corresponding crepant resolutions φ:𝒳⇢𝒳+\varphi\colon{\mathcal{X}}\dashrightarrow{\mathcal{X}}^{+} over C′C^{\prime}. But then φ∗(ℒ+)∼C′ℒ\varphi^{*}({\mathcal{L}}^{+})\sim_{C^{\prime}}{\mathcal{L}}, so φ\varphi descends to an isomorphism φ¯′:𝒳¯′→𝒳¯+′\overline{\varphi}\,\!^{\prime}\colon\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\,\!^{\prime}\to\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\,\!^{+}\,\!{}^{\prime} of the relatively ample models of ℒ{\mathcal{L}} and ℒ+{\mathcal{L}}^{+} over (C′,0)(C^{\prime},0). (For f:𝒳→Cf\colon{\mathcal{X}}\to C, the ample model of ℒ{\mathcal{L}} over CC is ProjC⊕d≥0f∗ℒd{\Proj}_{C}\oplus_{d\geq 0}f_{*}{\mathcal{L}}^{d}.) These relatively ample models 𝒳¯′\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\,\!^{\prime}, 𝒳¯+′\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\,\!^{+}\,\!{}^{\prime} are simply the base changes along (C′,0)→(C,0)(C^{\prime},0)\to(C,0) of 𝒳¯\overline{{\mathcal{X}}} and 𝒳¯+\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\,\!^{+}. Since φ¯′\overline{\varphi}^{\prime} is an isomorphism, we deduce that φ¯\overline{\varphi} is too, as φ¯′\overline{\varphi}^{\prime} is the base change of φ¯\overline{\varphi}.

3. Analytic moduli

We begin by setting the notation and reviewing fundamental results about analytic K3 surfaces. For general references, see [Huy16] or [Bea85].

The cup product endows H2​(X,ℤ)H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z}) with a symmetric bilinear form ⋅\cdot, making it isometric to the unique even unimodular lattice of signature (3,19)(3,19). Let Ω∈H0​(X,KX)\Omega\in H^{0}(X,K_{X}) denote a non-vanishing holomorphic 22-form on XX. Then there is a Hodge decomposition

H2​(X,ℂ)=H2,0​(X)⊕H1,1​(X)⊕H0,2​(X)H^{2}(X,\mathbb{C})=H^{2,0}(X)\oplus H^{1,1}(X)\oplus H^{0,2}(X)

with H2,0​(X)=ℂ​[Ω]H^{2,0}(X)=\mathbb{C}[\Omega] a complex line. It is orthogonal with respect to the Hodge form (α,β)↦α⋅β¯(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto\alpha\cdot\overline{\beta}. By the Lefschetz (1,1)(1,1)-theorem, the Néron–Severi group is

NS⁡(X)=H1,1​(X)∩H2​(X,ℤ)=[Ω]⟂∩H2​(X,ℤ).\operatorname{NS}(X)=H^{1,1}(X)\cap H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z})=[\Omega]^{\perp}\cap H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z}).

Here, H1,1​(X,ℝ)⊂H2​(X,ℝ)H^{1,1}(X,{\mathbb{R}})\subset H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{R}}) is [Ω]⟂:=⟨Re⁡Ω,Im⁡Ω⟩⟂[\Omega]^{\perp}:=\langle\operatorname{Re}\Omega,\operatorname{Im}\Omega\rangle^{\perp}. Because h1​(X)=0h^{1}(X)=0 and π1​(X)=1\pi_{1}(X)=1, we have NS⁡(X)=Pic⁡(X)\operatorname{NS}(X)={\rm Pic}(X).

Definition 3.1.

The roots of XX are the elements β∈NS⁡(X)\beta\in\operatorname{NS}(X) for which β2=−2\beta^{2}=-2. Associated to each root is a reflection rβ∈O⁡(H2​(X,ℤ))r_{\beta}\in O(H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z})) defined by

rβ​(v)=v+(v⋅β)​β.r_{\beta}(v)=v+(v\cdot\beta)\beta.

We define the Weyl group be the group WX:=⟨rβ:β a root of X⟩⊂O(H2(X,ℤ))W_{X}:=\langle r_{\beta}\,:\,\beta\textrm{ a root of }X\rangle\subset O(H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z})), generated by reflections in the roots.

Remark 3.2.

The group WXW_{X} may be infinite because the roots β\beta lie in a vector space H1,1​(X,ℝ)H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb{R}) of hyperbolic signature (1,19)(1,19), and may be infinite in number.

Definition 3.3.

The Kähler cone 𝒦X⊂H1,1​(X,ℝ)\mathcal{K}_{X}\subset H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb{R}) is the set of classes of Kähler forms on XX. Denote by 𝒦¯X⊂H1,1​(X,ℝ)\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X}\subset H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb{R}) the closure of 𝒦X\mathcal{K}_{X} in the set of positive norm vectors.

Every K3 admits a Kähler form [Siu83]. There are two connected components 𝒞X⊔(−𝒞X)⊂H1,1​(X,ℝ)\mathcal{C}_{X}\sqcup(-\mathcal{C}_{X})\subset H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb{R}) of positive norm vectors, which are distinguished by the property 𝒦X⊂𝒞X\mathcal{K}_{X}\subset\mathcal{C}_{X}. We call 𝒞X\mathcal{C}_{X} the positive cone. Then 𝒦¯X\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X} is a fundamental chamber for the action of WXW_{X} on 𝒞X\mathcal{C}_{X}. We may now state the (first part of the) Torelli theorem:

Theorem 3.4 ([PSS71, BR75, LP81]).

Two analytic K3 surfaces XX and X′X^{\prime} are isomorphic if and only if they are Hodge-isometric, i.e. there exists an isometry i:H2​(X′,ℤ)→H2​(X,ℤ)i:H^{2}(X^{\prime},\mathbb{Z})\to H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z}) for which i⁡(H2,0​(X′))=H2,0​(X)i(H^{2,0}(X^{\prime}))=H^{2,0}(X). Furthermore, i=f∗i=f^{*} for an isomorphism f:X→X′f:X\to X^{\prime} if and only if i⁡(𝒦X′)=𝒦Xi(\mathcal{K}_{X^{\prime}})=\mathcal{K}_{X}. This isomorphism ff is uniquely determined by ii.

Note that ±1\pm 1 and g∈WXg\in W_{X} act by Hodge isometries on H2​(X,ℤ)H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z}). For any Hodge isometry ii between X′X^{\prime} and XX, there is a unique sign and unique element g∈WXg\in W_{X} such that ±g∘i(𝒦X′)=𝒦X\pm g\circ i(\mathcal{K}_{X^{\prime}})=\mathcal{K}_{X} in which case, there is an isomorphism f:X→X′f:X\to X^{\prime} satisfying f∗=±g∘if^{*}=\pm g\circ i. Thus, the group of Hodge isometries of XX fits into a split exact sequence of groups

(1) 0→{±1}×WX→HodgeIsom⁡(X)→Aut⁡(X)→0.\displaystyle 0\to\{\pm 1\}\times W_{X}\to{\rm HodgeIsom}(X)\to{\rm Aut}(X)\to 0.
Definition 3.5.

Let LK​3:=I​I3,19=U⊕3⊕E8⊕2L_{K3}:=I\!I_{3,19}=U^{\oplus 3}\oplus E_{8}^{\oplus 2} be a fixed copy of the unique even unimodular lattice of signature (3,19)(3,19), i.e. the K3 lattice.

Here, U=I​I1,1U=I\!I_{1,1}, and our convention is that E8E_{8} is negative-definite.

Definition 3.6.

Let π:𝒳→S\pi\colon\mathcal{X}\to S be a family of smooth analytic K3 surfaces over an analytic space SS. A marking is an isometry of local systems μ:R2​π∗​ℤ¯→L¯K​3\mu\colon R^{2}\pi_{*}\underline{\mathbb{Z}}\to\underline{L}_{K3}.

An analytic family 𝒳→S\mathcal{X}\to S admits a marking if and only if the monodromy of the Gauss-Manin connection is trivial. If SS is a point, then 𝒳=X\mathcal{X}=X is a K3 surface together with an isometry μ:H2​(X,ℤ)→LK​3\mu\colon H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z})\to L_{K3}. A marking over a single fiber extends canonically to a marking over any simply connected base SS.

Definition 3.7.

An isomorphism of marked K3 surfaces f:(X,μ)→(X′,μ′)f:(X,\mu)\to(X^{\prime},\mu^{\prime}) is an isomorphism f:X→X′f:X\to X^{\prime} such that μ∘f∗=μ′\mu\circ f^{*}=\mu^{\prime}.

Note that marked K3 surfaces have no nontrivial automorphisms: By Theorem 3.4, the homomorphism Aut⁡(X)→O⁡(H2​(X,ℤ)){\rm Aut}(X)\to O(H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z})) is faithful.

Definition 3.8.

The period domain of analytic K3 surfaces is

𝔻:=ℙ{x∈LK​3⊗ℂ:x⋅x=0,x⋅x¯>0}.\mathbb{D}:=\mathbb{P}\{x\in L_{K3}\otimes\mathbb{C}\,:\,x\cdot x=0,\,x\cdot\overline{x}>0\}.

It is an analytic open subset of a 2020-dimensional quadric in ℙ21\mathbb{P}^{21}. Let (𝒳→S,μ)(\mathcal{X}\to S,\,\mu) be a marked family of K3 surfaces. The period map PP is defined by

P:S→𝔻,s↦μ⁡(H2,0​(Xs)).P\colon S\to\mathbb{D},\quad s\mapsto\mu(H^{2,0}(X_{s})).

Since H0​(X,TX)=H2​(X,TX)=0H^{0}(X,T_{X})=H^{2}(X,T_{X})=0, the deformation theory of compact complex manifolds [Kod86], [Kod64, Theorem 17] implies the existence of a Kuranishi family:

Theorem 3.9.

Let (X,μ)(X,\mu) be a marked K3 surface. There exists a family of K3 surfaces 𝒳→U\mathcal{X}\to U over a complex analytic ball U⊂ℂ20U\subset\mathbb{C}^{20}, which defines a universal deformation of XX, and such that the induced period map P:U→𝔻P\colon U\to\mathbb{D} is an isomorphism onto its image.

Recall that an analytic deformation π:𝒳→(U,0)\pi\colon\mathcal{X}\to(U,0) of the fiber X=π−1​(0)X=\pi^{-1}(0) is universal if it is the final object in the category of germs of deformations of XX. That is, given any flat family deforming XX over a base (B,b)(B,b), there is a sufficiently small analytic neighborhood of the point b∈Bb\in B over which XX fibers, such that the restricted family is the pullback of π\pi along a unique map (B,b)→(U,0)(B,b)\to(U,0).

Corollary 3.10.

A family of marked K3 surfaces 𝒳→S\mathcal{X}\to S over a smooth base SS is universal at every fiber XsX_{s} where the differential d​P:Ts​S→TP⁡(s)​𝔻dP:T_{s}S\to T_{P(s)}\mathbb{D} of the period map is an isomorphism.

From these facts one may construct the moduli space of marked analytic K3 surfaces by gluing together deformation spaces, as in [BR75, LP81, Bea85].

Theorem 3.11.

There exists a fine moduli space ℳ{\mathcal{M}} of marked analytic K3 surfaces, a non-separated, smooth complex analytic space of dimension 2020 endowed with an étale period map P:ℳ→𝔻P\colon{\mathcal{M}}\to{\mathbb{D}}, admitting a universal family 𝒳→ℳ\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{M}.

Sketch.

For every isomorphism type (X,μ)(X,\mu) of marked K3 surface, construct a Kuranishi family 𝒳(X,μ)→U(X,μ)\mathcal{X}_{(X,\mu)}\to U_{(X,\mu)} over a contractible base, which is universal at all fibers (cf. Corollary 3.10), and extend the marking μ\mu on XX to the family. Then glue together these deformation spaces

ℳ:=⋃(X,μ)U(X,μ)\mathcal{M}:=\bigcup_{(X,\mu)}U_{(X,\mu)}

by gluing U(X,μ)U_{(X,\mu)} and U(X′,μ′)U_{(X^{\prime},\mu^{\prime})} along the subset parameterizing isomorphic marked K3 surfaces. This subset is open because the family over U(X,μ)U_{(X,\mu)} is universal at every point, and the germ of a universal deformation is unique.

Since marked K3 surfaces have no nontrivial automorphisms, there is a unique way to glue the two families 𝒳(X,μ)→U(X,μ)\mathcal{X}_{(X,\mu)}\to U_{(X,\mu)} and 𝒳(X′,μ′)→U(X′,μ′)\mathcal{X}_{(X^{\prime},\mu^{\prime})}\to U_{(X^{\prime},\mu^{\prime})} along this common open subset. So there exists a family 𝒳→ℳ\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{M} of marked analytic K3 surfaces. Since we ranged over every isomorphism type and the universality holds at every point of ℳ\mathcal{M}, any marked family of analytic K3 surfaces is pulled back uniquely from 𝒳→ℳ\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{M}. So ℳ\mathcal{M} is a fine moduli space. ∎

The second part of the Torelli theorem is surjectivity of the period map:

Theorem 3.12 ([Tod80]).

The period map P:ℳ→𝔻P\colon\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{D} is surjective.

Let x∈𝔻x\in\mathbb{D} and define Wx:=⟨rβ:β∈x⟂∩LK​3,β2=−2⟩W_{x}:=\langle r_{\beta}\,:\,\beta\in x^{\perp}\cap L_{K3},\,\beta^{2}=-2\rangle. If P⁡(X,μ)=xP(X,\mu)=x, then WXW_{X} and WxW_{x} are identified via μ\mu, since NS⁡(X)=H2,0​(X)⟂∩H2​(X,ℤ){\rm NS}(X)=H^{2,0}(X)^{\perp}\cap H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{Z}}). By Theorems 3.4, 3.12 and the description of the Kähler cone, we have:

Corollary 3.13.

Let x∈𝔻x\in\mathbb{D} be a period. Then P−1​(x)P^{-1}(x) is a torsor over {±1}×Wx\{\pm 1\}\times W_{x} with action given by (X,μ)↦(X,g∘μ)(X,\mu)\mapsto(X,g\circ\mu).

The moduli space ℳ=ℳ1⊔ℳ2\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}_{1}\sqcup\mathcal{M}_{2} consists of two disjoint components, interchanged by μ↦−μ\mu\mapsto-\mu, because the monodromy of the universal family does not permute the decomposition of positive norm vectors in H1,1​(X,ℝ)H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb{R}) into components 𝒞X⊔(−𝒞X)\mathcal{C}_{X}\sqcup(-\mathcal{C}_{X}).

4. Quasipolarized moduli

We now give analogous definitions to Section 3 in the Λ\Lambda-quasipolarized case. The standard reference here is [Dol96]. However, Thm. 3.1 in ibid. is incorrect, see Remark 4.24. We give an alternative definition of a lattice-polarized K3 surface for which [Dol96, Thm. 3.1] remains true.

Let J:Λ↪LK​3J\colon\Lambda\hookrightarrow L_{K3} be a fixed primitive, non-degenerate, hyperbolic sublattice of signature (1,r−1)(1,r-1) with r≤20r\leq 20. The construction depends on this embedding and not just on the abstract lattice Λ\Lambda. We require the following notion:

Definition 4.1.

A vector h∈Λ⊗ℝh\in\Lambda\otimes{\mathbb{R}} is very irrational if h∉Λ′⊗ℝh\notin\Lambda^{\prime}\otimes{\mathbb{R}} for any proper, saturated sublattice Λ′⊊Λ\Lambda^{\prime}\subsetneq\Lambda. We will henceforth take h∈Λ⊗ℝh\in\Lambda\otimes{\mathbb{R}} to be a fixed very irrational vector of positive norm h2>0h^{2}>0.

Definition 4.2.

A (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-quasipolarized K3 surface (X,j)(X,j) is a K3 surface XX, and a primitive lattice embedding j:Λ↪NS⁡(X)j\colon\Lambda\hookrightarrow\operatorname{NS}(X) for which j⁡(h)∈𝒦¯Xj(h)\in\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X} is big and nef. Two such (X,j)(X,j) and (X′,j′)(X^{\prime},j^{\prime}) are isomorphic if there is an isomorphism f:X→X′f\colon X\to X^{\prime} of K3 surfaces for which j=f∗∘j′j=f^{*}\circ j^{\prime}.

Remark 4.3.

Consider the set of roots β∈Λ\beta\in\Lambda and let W⁡(Λ):=⟨rβ⟩⊂O⁡(Λ)W(\Lambda):=\langle r_{\beta}\rangle\subset O(\Lambda) be the corresponding reflection group. Then hh distinguishes a connected component 𝒞Λ{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda} of the positive norm vectors, and an open cone 𝒦Λ⊂𝒞Λ{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}\subset\mathcal{C}_{\Lambda} whose closure 𝒦¯Λ\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{\Lambda} is a fundamental chamber for the action of W⁡(Λ)W(\Lambda) on 𝒞Λ{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda} that contains hh. The definition of a Λ\Lambda-quasipolarization jj in [Dol96] is that j⁡(𝒦Λ)j(\mathcal{K}_{\Lambda}) must contain a big and nef class. This condition is implied by j⁡(h)j(h) being big and nef, but is weaker.

Definition 4.2 and Dolgachev’s definition agree when NS⁡(X)=Λ\operatorname{NS}(X)=\Lambda. In fact, Proposition 4.14 implies that the definitions agree on a finite complement of Heegner divisors. But Remark 4.24 gives an example in which the two definitions differ, even for an ample (not just big and nef) quasipolarization.

Definition 4.4.

A marking of (X,j)(X,j) is an isometry μ:H2​(X,ℤ)→LK​3\mu:H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z})\to L_{K3} for which J=μ∘jJ=\mu\circ j.

Since jj is determined by μ\mu and JJ, it can be dropped from the notation. As J:Λ→LK​3J\colon\Lambda\to L_{K3} is a fixed embedding, we may identify Λ⊂LK​3\Lambda\subset L_{K3} with a fixed sublattice of the reference lattice LK​3L_{K3}. Then, im​j{\rm im}\,j is recovered as μ−1​(Λ)\mu^{-1}(\Lambda) and Definition 4.2 says that μ−1​(h)\mu^{-1}(h) is big and nef. Define the Λ\Lambda-quasipolarized period domain as

𝔻Λ:=ℙ{x∈Λ⟂⊗ℂ:x⋅x=0,x⋅x¯>0}.\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda}:=\mathbb{P}\{x\in\Lambda^{\perp}\otimes\mathbb{C}\,:\,x\cdot x=0,\,x\cdot\overline{x}>0\}.

Since any element of the Néron–Severi group NS⁡(X)⊂H2​(X,ℤ)\operatorname{NS}(X)\subset H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z}) is perpendicular to H2,0​(X)H^{2,0}(X), we have that 𝔻Λ\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda} contains the image of the period map on a family of marked Λ\Lambda-quasipolarized K3 surfaces (𝒳→S,μ)(\mathcal{X}\to S,\mu).

Definition 4.5.

Define the Weyl group of a point x∈𝔻Λx\in\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda} to be

Wx(Λ⟂):=⟨rβ:β∈x⟂∩Λ⟂⟩.W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}):=\langle r_{\beta}\,:\,\beta\in x^{\perp}\cap\Lambda^{\perp}\rangle.

Note that now Wx​(Λ⟂)W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}) is finite because Λ⟂∩H1,1​(X,ℝ)\Lambda^{\perp}\cap H^{1,1}(X,{\mathbb{R}}) is negative-definite.

Definition 4.6.

Let ℳ¯Λ,h\underline{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h} be the moduli functor of marked (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-quasipolarized K3 surfaces for a very irrational vector h∈Λ⊗ℝh\in\Lambda\otimes{\mathbb{R}}.

Theorem 4.7 shows that even though the moduli functor ℳ¯Λ,h\underline{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h} depends on the very irrational vector hh chosen, the space representing it doesn’t. Even the universal families are the same for small deformations of hh, by Remark 4.20.

Theorem 4.7.

For any choice of a very irrational vector hh, the moduli functor ℳ¯Λ,h\underline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{\Lambda,h} is represented by a non-separated, smooth complex analytic space ℳΛ,h{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h} of dimension 20−rank⁡Λ20-\rank\Lambda, endowed with an étale, generically one-to-one period map Ph:ℳΛ,h→𝔻ΛP_{h}\colon\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda,h}\to{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}. admitting a universal family fh:(𝒳h,μ)→ℳΛ,hf_{h}\colon({\mathcal{X}}_{h},\mu)\to\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda,h}. For any x∈𝔻Λx\in{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}, the fiber Ph−1​(x)P_{h}^{-1}(x) is a torsor over the finite group Wx​(Λ⟂)W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}).

For different very irrational vectors h1,h2h_{1},h_{2}, the moduli spaces ℳΛ,h1{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h_{1}}, ℳΛ,h2{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h_{2}} are canonically isomorphic, so they can be identified with a fixed complex manifold, which we denote ℳΛ{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda}.

The proof is a modification of that of [Dol96, Thm. 3.1].

Proof.

First, consider the unpolarized period map for marked analytic K3 surfaces

P:ℳ→𝔻P:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{D}

and take the sublocus P−1​(𝔻Λ)P^{-1}(\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda}). This is identified with the moduli space of marked K3 surfaces (X,μ)(X,\mu) for which μ−1​(Λ)⊂Pic​(X)\mu^{-1}(\Lambda)\subset{\rm Pic}(X). Let x∈𝔻Λx\in\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda} and choose (X,μ)∈P−1​(x)(X,\mu)\in P^{-1}(x) arbitrarily. The action of g∈{±1}×Wxg\in\{\pm 1\}\times W_{x} on the fiber is (X,μ)↦(X,g∘μ).(X,\mu)\mapsto(X,g\circ\mu). Since μ⁡(𝒦¯X)\mu(\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X}) is a fundamental domain for the action of {±1}×Wx\{\pm 1\}\times W_{x} on the positive norm vectors in x⟂⊂LK​3⊗ℝx^{\perp}\subset L_{K3}\otimes{\mathbb{R}}, there exists some gg for which h∈(g∘μ)​(𝒦¯X)h\in(g\circ\mu)(\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X}).

So we may as well have assumed μ\mu itself satisfies h∈μ⁡(𝒦¯X)h\in\mu(\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X}). Next, we claim that the set of g∈Wxg\in W_{x} for which h∈(g∘μ)​(𝒦¯X)h\in(g\circ\mu)(\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X}) is equal to Wx​(Λ⟂)⊂WxW_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp})\subset W_{x}. Certainly any element g∈Wx​(Λ⟂)g\in W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}) preserves this condition, because g|Λ=idΛg|_{\Lambda}={\rm id}_{\Lambda} and so g⁡(h)=hg(h)=h. Conversely, since WxW_{x} is a reflection group, any such element gg is generated by reflections in roots β∈h⟂\beta\in h^{\perp}. But the integral classes in h⟂h^{\perp} are exactly the integral classes in Λ⟂\Lambda^{\perp} because hh is very irrational. (This is the point of choosing a very irrational vector hh.) So one has g∈Wx​(Λ⟂)g\in W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}).

Using the étale map of Theorem 3.11, we identify an open subset Ux,h⊂ℳΛ,hU_{x,h}\subset{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h} with an open subset of P−1​(𝔻Λ)P^{-1}({\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}) in ℳ{\mathcal{M}}. Gluing these neighborhoods for all x∈𝔻Λx\in{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}, we build the fine moduli space ℳΛ,h{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h} as an open subset of P−1​(𝔻Λ)P^{-1}({\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}) together with a surjective period map to 𝔻Λ{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}.

For a vector β∈LK​3\beta\in L_{K3} one has β⋅x=0\beta\cdot x=0 for all x∈𝔻Λx\in{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda} if and only if β∈Λ\beta\in\Lambda. Thus, for every root β∈Λ⟂\beta\in\Lambda^{\perp} the zero set β⟂⊂𝔻Λ\beta^{\perp}\subset{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda} is a proper closed subset. This implies that for any x∈𝔻Λx\in{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda} outside of a locally finite countable union of hyperplanes ∪β⟂\cup\beta^{\perp} with β\beta going over roots in Λ⟂\Lambda^{\perp}, one has Wx​(Λ⟂)=1W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp})=1. So, PP is generically one-to-one.

Let h1,h2h_{1},h_{2} be two very irrational vectors. A point y1∈Ph1−1​(x)y_{1}\in P_{h_{1}}^{-1}(x) corresponds to a K3 surface Y1Y_{1} whose period is xx. It defines a fundamental chamber ℭy1{\mathfrak{C}}_{y_{1}} in the vector space x⟂∩(Λ⟂⊗ℝ)x^{\perp}\cap(\Lambda^{\perp}\otimes~{\mathbb{R}}) for the reflection group Wx​(Λ⟂)W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}): the positive chamber for the positive roots on Y1Y_{1} which lie in Λ⟂\Lambda^{\perp}. The choice of such a Wx​(Λ⟂)W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp})-chamber realizes the Wx​(Λ⟂)W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp})-torsor structure on Ph1−1​(x)P_{h_{1}}^{-1}(x).

The same is true for the points y2∈Ph2−1​(x)y_{2}\in P_{h_{2}}^{-1}(x). Thus there is a canonical isomorphism of the torsors Ph1−1​(x)→Ph2−1​(x)P_{h_{1}}^{-1}(x)\to P_{h_{2}}^{-1}(x) defined by sending y1↦y2y_{1}\mapsto y_{2} if and only if ℭy1=ℭy2{\mathfrak{C}}_{y_{1}}={\mathfrak{C}}_{y_{2}}. This defines a canonical biholomorphism ℳΛ,h1→ℳΛ,h2{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h_{1}}\to{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h_{2}} and we deduce the independence of ℳΛ,h{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h} on hh as a complex manifold. ∎

So ℳ¯Λ,h\underline{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h} is represented by a submanifold ℳΛ,h⊂ℳ\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda,h}\subset\mathcal{M} of the space of all marked K3 surfaces, and ℳΛ,h≃ℳΛ\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda,h}\simeq\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda} for all very irrational hh. Thus, we may make identifications ℳ¯Λ,h=ℳΛ,h=ℳΛ\underline{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h}=\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda,h}=\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda} unless we need to either to distinguish the functors ℳ¯Λ,h\underline{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h} for different hh, or distinguish the subloci ℳΛ,h⊂ℳ\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda,h}\subset\mathcal{M}.

Corollary 4.8.

Let ℳΛ,h∘⊂ℳΛ,h{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h}^{\circ}\subset{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h} denote the moduli space of marked (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-quasipolarized K3 surfaces (X,μ)(X,\mu) for which μ⁡(h)\mu(h) is ample. Then PP restricts to an isomorphism from ℳΛ,h∘{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h}^{\circ} to the complement of Heegner divisors

𝔻Λ∘:={x∈𝔻Λ:x⋅β≠0​ for all roots ​β∈Λ⟂}.{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}^{\circ}:=\{x\in{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}\,:\,x\cdot\beta\neq 0\textrm{ for all roots }\beta\in\Lambda^{\perp}\}.

The corollary is a modification of [Dol96, Cor. 3.2].

Proof.

By definition, μ⁡(h)\mu(h) is big and nef. It is ample if and only if there does not exist a root β∈NS⁡(X)\beta\in\operatorname{NS}(X) with β⋅μ⁡(h)=0\beta\cdot\mu(h)=0 Since hh is very irrational, we would necessarily have β∈Λ⟂\beta\in\Lambda^{\perp}. Thus, μ⁡(h)\mu(h) is ample exactly when Wx​(Λ⟂)=1W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp})=1, and the corollary follows from Theorem 4.7. ∎

Definition 4.9.

The small cones in 𝒞Λ∪(−𝒞Λ){\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}\cup(-{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}), which we will denote by σ\sigma, are the connected components of the complements of the perpendiculars of every vector β∈LK​3∖Λ⟂\beta\in L_{K3}\setminus\Lambda^{\perp} of square β2=−2\beta^{2}=-2 for which ⟨Λ,β⟩⊂LK​3\langle\Lambda,\beta\rangle\subset L_{K3} is hyperbolic, i.e. it is nondegenerate of signature (1,s)(1,s) for some s∈ℤ≥0s\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}.

Remark 4.10.

Definition 4.9 is the key definition of this paper. In [Dol96], a cone 𝒦Λ{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda} is defined as an open Weyl chamber for the Weyl group W⁡(Λ)W(\Lambda) and a “Λ\Lambda-polarized quasi ample” K3 surface is defined as a pair (X,j)(X,j) with an embedding j:Λ↪NS⁡(X)j\colon\Lambda\hookrightarrow{\rm NS}(X) for which j⁡(𝒦Λ)j({\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}) contains a big and nef class. This is the main source of trouble, since the walls of the Kähler cone 𝒦X{\mathcal{K}}_{X} are determined by all roots β∈LK​3\beta\in L_{K3}, not just by those that lie in Λ\Lambda. The cones 𝒦X{\mathcal{K}}_{X} are too “large”, in that there may be too many isometries j:Λ→NS⁡(X)j\colon\Lambda\to{\rm NS}(X) for which j⁡(𝒦Λ)j({\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}) contains a big and nef class, leading in some cases to an infinite period fiber, see Remark 4.24.

Replacing 𝒦Λ{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda} with a small cone obviates the issue, doing what the choices of chambers were intended for in [Dol96]; see Proposition 4.17 and Theorem 4.7.

Remark 4.11.

The fact that the definition of a lattice-polarized K3 surface is somewhat delicate and requires care was known to experts for a long time. For example, it was one reason for introducing the notion of a “good embedding” in [Loo84, Section 4.2]. The issues with the original definition have been bypassed in different ways by some authors, for instance in [Jou16] and [Cam16, Cam18], by introducing the notion of 𝒦Λ{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}-generality, employed e.g. in [BCS19, BC23, Bas23].

For the following examples, we note that any even lattice of rank ≤3\leq 3 admits a primitive embedding into LK​3L_{K3}, and if rank ≤2\leq 2 then this embedding is unique modulo O⁡(LK​3)O(L_{K3}) by a theorem of James [Jam72], cf. [LP81, Thm. 2.4].

Example 4.12.

Let Λ=U⁡(n)=⟨e,f⟩\Lambda=U(n)=\langle e,f\rangle with e2=f2=0e^{2}=f^{2}=0 and e⋅f=n>0e\cdot f=n>0. Consider a lattice ⟨Λ,β⟩\langle\Lambda,\beta\rangle such that β2=−2\beta^{2}=-2, β⋅e=a\beta\cdot e=a, β⋅f=−b\beta\cdot f=-b. The hyperplane β⟂\beta^{\perp} intersects the union 𝒞Λ∪(−𝒞Λ){\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}\cup(-\mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}) of the first and third quadrants of Λ\Lambda iff a​b>0ab>0. If β∉Λ\beta\not\in\Lambda, this lattice is hyperbolic if and only if a​b<nab<n. The case β∈Λ\beta\in\Lambda is possible only for n=1n=1, then a​b=1ab=1. We see that in the case Λ=U\Lambda=U (corresponding to elliptic K3 surfaces with a section) the small cone decomposition coincides with the Weyl chamber decomposition for W⁡(Λ)W(\Lambda). However, they are different for n≥2n\geq 2. In this case, there are only finitely many small cones. For n≥2n\geq 2 the lattice Λ\Lambda has no roots, so W⁡(Λ)=1W(\Lambda)=1 and 𝒦Λ=𝒞Λ{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}={\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}.

Example 4.13.

Similarly, let Λ=⟨e1,e2⟩\Lambda=\langle e_{1},e_{2}\rangle be an even hyperbolic lattice with the quadratic form q⁡(x,y)=2​n​(x2−d​y2)q(x,y)=2n(x^{2}-dy^{2}), with n,d∈ℕn,d\in{\mathbb{N}} and non-square dd. Consider a lattice ⟨Λ,β⟩\langle\Lambda,\beta\rangle such that β2=−2\beta^{2}=-2, β⋅e1=a\beta\cdot e_{1}=a and β⋅e2=b\beta\cdot e_{2}=b. The hyperplane β⟂\beta^{\perp} intersects 𝒞Λ∪(−𝒞Λ){\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}\cup(-{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}) iff b2−d​a2>0b^{2}-da^{2}>0. If β∉Λ\beta\not\in\Lambda then ⟨Λ,β⟩\langle\Lambda,\beta\rangle is hyperbolic iff b2−d​a2<4​d​nb^{2}-da^{2}<4dn. The case β∈Λ\beta\in\Lambda is possible only for n=1n=1, in which case b2−d​a2=4​db^{2}-da^{2}=4d. In all cases, the infinitely many solutions of Pell’s equations b2−d​a2=kb^{2}-da^{2}=k with 0<k<4​d​n0<k<4dn give infinitely many walls of small cones. So, in this case there are infinitely many small cones. On the other hand, for n≥2n\geq 2 the lattice Λ\Lambda has no roots, so W⁡(Λ)=1W(\Lambda)=1 and 𝒦Λ=𝒞Λ{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}={\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}.

The lattice vectors λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda are in bijection with the algebraic integers x+y​d∈ℤ⁡[d]x+y\sqrt{d}\in{\mathbb{Z}}[\sqrt{d}], and multiplying by a number with norm N⁡(x+y​d)=x2−d​y2=1N(x+y\sqrt{d})=x^{2}-dy^{2}=1 is an isometry of Λ\Lambda. This implies that modulo the isometry group O⁡(Λ)O(\Lambda) there are only finitely many small cones.

Proposition 4.14.

The small cone decomposition is locally rational polyhedral. Let GΛ⊂O⁡(LK3)G_{\Lambda}\subset O(L_{\rm K3}) be the group of isometries of LK3L_{\rm K3} that preserve Λ\Lambda. The number of GΛG_{\Lambda}-orbits of small cones is finite.

Proof.

First, we show that the walls of the small cone decomposition are locally finite in 𝒞Λ∪(−𝒞Λ){\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}\cup(-{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}). Write β=βΛ+βΛ⟂\beta=\beta_{\Lambda}+\beta_{\Lambda^{\perp}} with βΛ∈Λ⊗ℚ\beta_{\Lambda}\in\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{Q} and βΛ⟂∈Λ⟂⊗ℚ\beta_{\Lambda^{\perp}}\in\Lambda^{\perp}\otimes\mathbb{Q}. Note that βΛ⟂\beta_{\Lambda^{\perp}} lies in the hyperbolic space ⟨Λ,β⟩⊗ℚ\langle\Lambda,\beta\rangle\otimes\mathbb{Q} and is perpendicular to Λ\Lambda, so we necessarily have (βΛ⟂)2≤0(\beta_{\Lambda^{\perp}})^{2}\leq 0. Thus, (βΛ)2≥−2(\beta_{\Lambda})^{2}\geq-2.

Next, observe that βΛ∈Λ∗\beta_{\Lambda}\in\Lambda^{*} lies in the dual lattice, because intersecting with β\beta defines an integral linear functional on Λ\Lambda. The hyperplane (βΛ)⟂(\beta_{\Lambda})^{\perp} intersects the positive cone 𝒞Λ{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda} only if βΛ2<0\beta_{\Lambda}^{2}<0. Since Λ\Lambda has a finite index in Λ∗\Lambda^{*}, for the βΛ\beta_{\Lambda} defining a wall, there are only finitely many possible values that (βΛ)2(\beta_{\Lambda})^{2} can take, and the set of such vectors in Λ∗\Lambda^{*} is discrete. The first statement of the proposition follows.

Now, observe that GΛG_{\Lambda} is a finite index subgroup of O⁡(Λ)O(\Lambda). Let 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} be a polyhedral fundamental domain with finitely many sides for the action of GΛG_{\Lambda} on the projectivization of the positive norm vectors ℍrank⁡Λ−1≃ℙ⁡(𝒞Λ∪(−𝒞Λ))=ℙ​𝒞Λ{\mathbb{H}}^{\rank\Lambda-1}\simeq{\mathbb{P}}({\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}\cup(-{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}))={\mathbb{P}}{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}. It exists by [Bow93, Prop. 5.6].

If rank⁡Λ≥3\rank\Lambda\geq 3 or Λ\Lambda is anisotropic then this polyhedron 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} has finite volume by a theorem of Borel and Harish-Chandra [BHC62, 7.8, 9.4]. Adding finitely many cusps gives a compact space 𝒫¯\overline{{\mathcal{P}}}. The set of hyperplanes β⟂\beta^{\perp} cuts it into finitely many cones. This implies the second statement of the proposition.

In the case of rank⁡Λ=2\rank\Lambda=2 the cone 𝒞Λ{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda} is isomorphic to a quadrant in ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} that is possibly divided into infinitely many small cones accumulating to the boundary. It is well known and easy to prove that the set of O⁡(Λ)O(\Lambda)-orbits of vectors of a given norm in Λ\Lambda is finite. This implies that the set of the O⁡(Λ)O(\Lambda)-orbits of the rays of these cones is finite, so there are only finitely many O⁡(Λ)O(\Lambda)-orbits of the small cones. ∎

Corollary 4.15.

For any hyperbolic lattice Λ\Lambda, if there is more than one small cone then there are infinitely many, unless Λ\Lambda is isotropic of rank 22.

Proof.

By the proof of Proposition 4.14, under these assumptions there is finite volume polyhedral fundamental domain 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} for the action of GΛG_{\Lambda}. If there is one wall β⟂\beta^{\perp} separating two small cones then it intersects some polyhedron g⁡(𝒫)g({\mathcal{P}}) in the GΛG_{\Lambda}-orbit of 𝒫{\mathcal{P}}. Then there are infinitely many walls g′​(β⟂)g^{\prime}(\beta^{\perp}) for g′∈GΛg^{\prime}\in G_{\Lambda}, so there are infinitely many small cones. ∎

On the other hand, if Λ\Lambda has no roots, then there is only one W⁡(Λ)W(\Lambda)-Weyl chamber 𝒦Λ=𝒞Λ{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}={\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}. So, for many lattices Λ\Lambda, a single Weyl chamber subdivides into infinitely many small cones. On the opposite side of the spectrum, we have:

Lemma 4.16.

Let Λ\Lambda be unimodular, i.e. isomorphic to UU, U⊕E8U\oplus E_{8} or U⊕E82U\oplus E_{8}^{2}. Then the small cones coincide with the Weyl chambers.

Proof.

Since Λ\Lambda is unimodular, it splits off as a direct summand: ⟨Λ,β⟩=Λ⊕B\langle\Lambda,\beta\rangle=\Lambda\oplus B. As in the proof of Proposition 4.14, β⟂\beta^{\perp} intersects the positive cone 𝒞Λ{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda} only if (βΛ)2<0(\beta_{\Lambda})^{2}<0. Since BB is negative definite, one has (βΛ⟂)2≤0(\beta_{\Lambda^{\perp}})^{2}\leq 0. The equality (βΛ⟂)2+(βΛ)2=−2(\beta_{\Lambda^{\perp}})^{2}+(\beta_{\Lambda})^{2}=-2 leaves the only possibility βΛ2=−2\beta_{\Lambda}^{2}=-2 and (βΛ⟂)2=0(\beta_{\Lambda^{\perp}})^{2}=0, which implies βΛ⟂=0\beta_{\Lambda^{\perp}}=0. So β∈Λ\beta\in\Lambda and β⟂\beta^{\perp} is a wall of a Weyl chamber. ∎

Proposition 4.17.

Let XX be a K3 surface, and let j:Λ↪Pic⁡(X)j:\Lambda\hookrightarrow{\rm Pic}(X) be an embedding. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    j⁡(h)∈𝒦¯Xj(h)\in\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X} i.e. jj defines an (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-quasipolarization.

  2. (2)

    j⁡(σ)⊂𝒦¯Xj(\sigma)\subset\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X} for the unique small cone σ\sigma containing hh.

  3. (3)

    For any h′∈σh^{\prime}\in\sigma in the same small cone as hh, j⁡(h′)∈𝒦¯Xj(h^{\prime})\in\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X}.

Observe that (3) holds, whether or not h′h^{\prime} is very irrational.

Proof.

The proposition follows from the statement that any wall of 𝒦¯X\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X} is of the form β⟂\beta^{\perp} for a root β∈H2​(X,ℤ)\beta\in H^{2}(X,{\mathbb{Z}}) and that the lattice ⟨j⁡(Λ),β⟩⊂NS⁡(X)⊂H1,1​(X,ℝ)\langle j(\Lambda),\beta\rangle\subset\operatorname{NS}(X)\subset H^{1,1}(X,{\mathbb{R}}) has hyperbolic signature for any root β\beta. The walls of 𝒦¯X\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X} associated to roots β∈j​(Λ)⟂\beta\in j(\Lambda)^{\perp} do not decompose Λ\Lambda. ∎

Proposition 4.18.

For two very irrational vectors h1,h2h_{1},h_{2}, the universal families fh1:(𝒳h1,μ)→ℳΛf_{h_{1}}\colon({\mathcal{X}}_{h_{1}},\mu)\to\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda} and fh2:(𝒳h2,μ)→ℳΛf_{h_{2}}\colon({\mathcal{X}}_{h_{2}},\mu)\to\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda} of marked K3 surfaces are isomorphic if and only if h1,h2h_{1},h_{2} lie in the same small cone σ\sigma.

Proof.

By Proposition 4.17, ℳh1⊂ℳ{\mathcal{M}}_{h_{1}}\subset{\mathcal{M}} and ℳh2⊂ℳ{\mathcal{M}}_{h_{2}}\subset{\mathcal{M}} are the same subset whenever h1,h2h_{1},h_{2} lie in the same small cone. Conversely, suppose h1,h2h_{1},h_{2} lie in distinct small cones. Then there exists a root β∈LK​3\beta\in L_{K3} for which ⟨Λ,β⟩⊂LK​3\langle\Lambda,\beta\rangle\subset L_{K3} is hyperbolic, β⋅h1>0\beta\cdot h_{1}>0, and β⋅h2<0\beta\cdot h_{2}<0. By the hyperbolicity of ⟨Λ,β⟩\langle\Lambda,\beta\rangle, the period domain 𝔻⟨Λ,β⟩⊂𝔻Λ{\mathbb{D}}_{\langle\Lambda,\beta\rangle}\subset{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda} is non-empty. So by Theorem 4.7, there exists a marked K3 surface (X,μ)∈ℳh1(X,\mu)\in{\mathcal{M}}_{h_{1}} for which the Néron–Severi group satifies ⟨Λ,β⟩⊂μ⁡(NS⁡(X))\langle\Lambda,\beta\rangle\subset\mu({\rm NS}(X)). In particular, μ−1​(β)\mu^{-1}(\beta) represents an effective class on XX, and so (X,μ)∉ℳh2(X,\mu)\notin{\mathcal{M}}_{h_{2}} as β⋅h2<0\beta\cdot h_{2}<0. Thus ℳh1≠ℳh2{\mathcal{M}}_{h_{1}}\neq{\mathcal{M}}_{h_{2}} as subsets of ℳ{\mathcal{M}}.

Since ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is a fine moduli space of marked K3 surfaces, the statement follows. ∎

As we see, the true datum in the definition of lattice quasipolarized K3 surfaces is a small cone σ\sigma, and an alternative notation for the moduli functor is ℳ¯Λ,σ\underline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{\Lambda,\sigma} for the moduli functor of marked (Λ,σ)(\Lambda,\sigma)-polarized K3 surfaces.

Remark 4.19.

Since the number of GΛG_{\Lambda}-orbits of small cones is finite by Proposition 4.14, there is a sense in which the number of moduli spaces of (Λ,σ)(\Lambda,\sigma)-quasipolarized K3 surfaces for a fixed lattice Λ\Lambda is finite. An isometry g∈GΛ⊂O⁡(LK3)g\in G_{\Lambda}\subset O(L_{\rm K3}) defines a natural transformation ℳ¯Λ,σ→ℳ¯Λ,g⁡(σ)\underline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{\Lambda,\sigma}\to\underline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{\Lambda,g(\sigma)} of moduli functors, given on objects by (X,μ)↦(X,g∘μ)(X,\mu)\mapsto(X,g\circ\mu).

Remark 4.20.

A primitive integral vector LL of positive norm L2L^{2}, in the closure of σ\sigma, defines a big and nef line bundle on every (Λ,σ)(\Lambda,\sigma)-quasipolarized K3 surface (X,j)(X,j). So any such LL defines an inclusion of ℳΛ,h↪ℳℤ​L\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda,h}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathbb{Z}L} by restriction j↦j|ℤ​Lj\mapsto j|_{\mathbb{Z}L}. Every L∈ΛL\in\Lambda of positive square lies in the closure of at least one, but possibly more than one, small cone.

If one defines ℳ¯Λ,h\underline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{\Lambda,h} as in Definition 4.2, but allowing any (not necessarily very irrational) choice of vector h∈Λ⊗ℝh\in\Lambda\otimes{\mathbb{R}}, h2>0h^{2}>0, then the space ℳΛ,h{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h} representing this functor is still a (non-separated) smooth complex analytic space of dimension 20−r20-r, as in Theorem 4.7. But the fiber of the period map is a finite union of Wx​(Λ⟂)W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp})-orbits, one for each small cone σ\sigma containing hh in its closure.

Definition 4.21.

Let ℱΛ,σq\mathcal{F}_{\Lambda,\sigma}^{\rm q} denote the moduli stack of (Λ,σ)(\Lambda,\sigma)-quasipolarized K3 surfaces, for a fixed small cone σ\sigma. Here q{\rm q} stands for “quasipolarized.”

Note that the families parameterized by ℱΛ,σq\mathcal{F}_{\Lambda,\sigma}^{\rm q} do not have a marking.

Theorem 4.22.

There is an isomorphism of stacks ℱΛ,σq=[ℳΛ,σ:Γ]\mathcal{F}_{\Lambda,\sigma}^{\rm q}=[\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda,\sigma}:\Gamma] where

Γ:={γ∈O⁡(LK​3):γ|Λ=idΛ}\Gamma:=\{\gamma\in O(L_{K3})\,:\,\gamma|_{\Lambda}={\rm id}_{\Lambda}\}

is the group of changes-of-marking. In particular, for different choices of the small cone σ\sigma these stacks are naturally isomorphic. The quotiented period map ℳΛ,σ/Γ→𝔻Λ/Γ\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda,\sigma}/\Gamma\to\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda}/\Gamma is a bijection.

Proof.

The first part follows formally from Theorem 4.7; note that for two small cones σ1,σ2\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2} the canonical isomorphism ℳΛ,σ1→ℳΛ,σ2{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,\sigma_{1}}\to{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,\sigma_{2}} is Γ\Gamma-equivariant. The second part follows from the fact that Γ⊃Wx​(Λ⟂)\Gamma\supset W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}) for any x∈𝔻Λx\in{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda} and so Γ\Gamma acts transitively on the fibers of the period map PP.∎

Remark 4.23.

The action of Γ\Gamma on 𝔻Λ\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda} (and thus also on ℳΛ\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda}) is properly discontinuous because 𝔻Λ\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda} is a Type IV Hermitian symmetric domain for the group Γℝ=O⁡(2,20−r)\Gamma_{\mathbb{R}}=O(2,20-r). So by the theorem of Baily-Borel [BB66], 𝔻Λ/Γ\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda}/\Gamma is a quasiprojective variety. The period domain 𝔻Λ\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda} has two connected components, interchanged by complex conjugation x↦x¯x\mapsto\overline{x}, and so the quotient by Γ\Gamma has either one or two connected components, depending on whether Γ\Gamma does or doesn’t have an element interchanging the two components of 𝔻Λ\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda}.

Remark 4.24.

As defined in [Dol96], the space of marked “Λ\Lambda-polarized quasi ample” K3s, using our notations, is

ℳΛ′:=⋃h∈𝒦ΛℳΛ,h=⋃σ⊂𝒦ΛℳΛ,σ⊂ℳ{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}:=\bigcup_{h\in{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}}{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,h}=\bigcup_{\sigma\subset{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}}{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda,\sigma}\subset{\mathcal{M}}

with hh ranging over all very irrational vectors, resp. with σ\sigma ranging over all small cones contained in a fixed open Weyl chamber 𝒦Λ⊂𝒞Λ{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}\subset{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda} for W⁡(Λ)W(\Lambda). Then [Dol96, Thm. 3.1] claims that P−1​(x)P^{-1}(x) is a torsor over the finite group Wx​(Λ⟂)W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}). In fact, with this definition, the fiber generally is not a torsor over any group, and it may be infinite if 𝒦Λ{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda} contains infinitely many small cones σ\sigma.

For example, start with a marked surface (X,μ)(X,\mu) with a period xx such that the lattice Pic⁡(X)\Pic(X) is reflective, e.g. U⊕E8U\oplus E_{8}. The chambers of the Weyl group WxW_{x} cover the positive cone of (U⊕E8)⊗ℝ(U\oplus E_{8})\otimes{\mathbb{R}} and projectivize to hyperbolic polytopes of finite volume. Let us assume that Λ⊂U⊕E8\Lambda\subset U\oplus E_{8} is a lattice of rank 22 and no roots, e.g. a lattice from Example 4.13. Then the condition that 𝒦Λ=𝒞Λ{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}={\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda} contain a big and nef class is equivalent to the condition that the hyperbolic line ℙ​𝒞Λ{\mathbb{P}}{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda} passes through the hyperbolic polytope

𝒫:=ℙ​μ​(𝒦¯X)∩(U⊕E8)⊗ℝ.\mathcal{P}:=\mathbb{P}\mu(\overline{{\mathcal{K}}}_{X})\cap(U\oplus E_{8})\otimes{\mathbb{R}}.

But any isometry g∈Wxg\in W_{x} for which g⁡(𝒫)∩ℙ​𝒞Λ≠∅g(\mathcal{P})\cap\mathbb{P}{\mathcal{C}}_{\Lambda}\neq\emptyset gives an “Λ\Lambda-polarized quasi-ample” K3 surface (X,g∘μ)(X,g\circ\mu) in the sense of [Dol96]. Each of these chambers gives a point in the fiber of the period map.

For an anisotropic Λ\Lambda, the set of such chambers is infinite. (Instead of a lattice or rank 22, one could also take a lattice with rank⁡Λ≥3\rank\Lambda\geq 3 to the same effect, cf. Corollary 4.15.) And for a generic Λ\Lambda, the set of such chambers is not naturally a torsor over any group. If, as in [Dol96], one defines the moduli space of Λ\Lambda-quasipolarized K3 surfaces to be ℱΛ′:=ℳΛ′/Γ{\mathcal{F}}^{\prime}_{\Lambda}:={\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}_{\Lambda}/\Gamma, then the map ℳ′/Γ→𝔻/Γ{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}/\Gamma\to{\mathbb{D}}/\Gamma is not a bijection. Instead, for the lattices Λ\Lambda in this example, this map has infinite fibers.

We can furthermore pick Λ\Lambda and xx in such a way that the Weyl group W⁡(x⟂∩Λ⟂)W(x^{\perp}\cap\Lambda^{\perp}) is trivial. Then the polarizations will be ample, not merely semiample.

For marked “Λ\Lambda-polarized ample K3 surfaces” as in [Dol96], the period map PP is only an isomorphism onto its image on the sublocus ℳΛ∘⁣∘⊂ℳΛ∘⊂ℳΛ{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda}^{\circ\circ}\subset{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda}^{\circ}\subset{\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda} where all roots β∈NS⁡(X)\beta\in\operatorname{NS}(X) satisfy β⟂∩𝒦Λ=∅\beta^{\perp}\cap{\mathcal{K}}_{\Lambda}=\emptyset. The image P⁡(ℳΛ∘⁣∘)P({\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda}^{\circ\circ}) is

𝔻Λ∘⁣∘:={x∈𝔻Λ:\displaystyle{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}^{\circ\circ}:=\{x\in{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}\,:\, x⋅β≠0​ for all roots ​β∈LK​3​ with\displaystyle x\cdot\beta\neq 0\textrm{ for all roots }\beta\in L_{K3}\textrm{ with }
⟨Λ,β⟩ hyperbolic and (βΛ)2<0}.\displaystyle\langle\Lambda,\beta\rangle\textrm{ hyperbolic and }(\beta_{\Lambda})^{2}<0\}.

This locus is a complement of finitely many Γ\Gamma-orbits of Heegner divisors in 𝔻Λ{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda} but it may contain the perpendiculars of vectors in Λ⟂\Lambda^{\perp} of norm not equal to −2-2. As in the proof of Proposition 4.14, the finiteness of Γ\Gamma-orbits follows from the fact that (βΛ⟂)2≥−2(\beta_{\Lambda^{\perp}})^{2}\geq-2, βΛ⟂⊂(Λ⟂)∗\beta_{\Lambda^{\perp}}\subset(\Lambda^{\perp})^{*}, and Λ⟂\Lambda^{\perp} has finite index in (Λ⟂)∗(\Lambda^{\perp})^{*}.

5. ADE moduli

We now describe a modification of the above moduli problems which produces a separated moduli space and stack. Theorem 5.5 below is known to experts, but to the authors’ knowledge there is no standard reference.

The notion of “lattice-polarized” is usually discussed only for smooth K3 surfaces as a special case of “lattice-quasipolarized”, as in Corollary 4.8. where it gives an open subset of 𝔻Λ/Γ{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}/\Gamma, the complement of hyperplanes α⟂\alpha^{\perp} for some some roots α\alpha. Here, instead we extend it to K3 surfaces with ADE singularities, and the coarse moduli space becomes the entire space 𝔻Λ/Γ{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}/\Gamma.

For us, a lattice-polarized ADE K3 surface is the ample model of a lattice-quasipolarized smooth K3 surface (X,j)(X,j), that is X¯=Proj⊕d≥0H0(X,Ld){\overline{X}}=\Proj\oplus_{d\geq 0}H^{0}(X,L^{d}), associated to a semiample line bundle L∈j⁡(Λ)L\in j(\Lambda).

In Definition 5.1 and Theorem 5.5, we begin with the case when hh, the first Chern class of LL, is generic, i.e. lies in some (open) small cone σ\sigma. Then, in Definition 5.6 and Corollary 5.10, we tackle the general case, when hh belongs to a face τ⊂σ¯\tau\subset\overline{\sigma} of a small cone, which we call a generalized small cone.

Definition 5.1.

Let h∈Λ⊗ℝh\in\Lambda\otimes{\mathbb{R}} be a vector contained in a small cone σ⊂Λ⊗ℝ\sigma\subset\Lambda\otimes{\mathbb{R}}.

A (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-polarized K3 surface (X¯,j)({\overline{X}},j) is a possibly singular surface X¯{\overline{X}} with at worst rational double point (ADE) singularities, whose minimal resolution X→X¯X\to{\overline{X}} is a smooth K3 surface, together with an isometric embedding j:Λ↪Pic⁡(X¯)j:\Lambda\hookrightarrow{\rm Pic}({\overline{X}}) for which j⁡(h)j(h) is ample.

A family of (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-polarized K3 surfaces is a flat family f:𝒳¯→Sf\colon\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\to S of K3 surfaces with at worst ADE singularities together with a homomorphism Λ→Pic𝒳¯/S⁡(S)\Lambda\to\Pic_{\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}/S}(S) such that every fiber is a (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-polarized K3 surface with ADE singularities.

For the same reasons as Propositions 4.17, 4.18, the functor of (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)- and (Λ,h′)(\Lambda,h^{\prime})-quasipolarized K3 surfaces is the same, for all hh, h′h^{\prime} in the same small cone σ\sigma. Thus, we may as well consider an h′∈σh^{\prime}\in\sigma which is integral. Then, for a (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-quasipolarized family 𝒳→S{\mathcal{X}}\to S, the SS-morphism 𝒳→𝒳¯{\mathcal{X}}\to\overline{{\mathcal{X}}} defined by passing to the ample model for h′h^{\prime} contracts all (−2)(-2)-curves in Λ⟂\Lambda^{\perp} and produces a (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-polarized family.

Remark 5.2.

In fact, if h1∈σ1h_{1}\in\sigma_{1} and h2∈σ2h_{2}\in\sigma_{2} lie in distinct small cones, the (Λ,h1)(\Lambda,h_{1})- and (Λ,h2)(\Lambda,h_{2})-polarized K3 surfaces X1,X2X_{1},X_{2} corresponding to a period x∈β⟂x\in\beta^{\perp}, for β\beta defining a wall separating h1h_{1} and h2h_{2}, are not isomorphic, since h1h_{1} is ample on X1X_{1} but not ample on X2X_{2}. For this reason, we cannot remove hh from the definition.

Consider a point x∈𝔻Λx\in{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}. The stabilizer Γx⊂Γ\Gamma_{x}\subset\Gamma of a point x∈𝔻Λx\in\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda} is the group of all Hodge isometries that fix the embedding J:Λ↪LK​3J:\Lambda\hookrightarrow L_{K3}. But the only Hodge isometries that are induced by automorphisms are those that preserve the Kähler cone. Thus there is an exact sequence of groups

0→Wx​(Λ⟂)→Γx→Aut⁡(X¯,j)→00\to W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp})\to\Gamma_{x}\to{\rm Aut}(\overline{X},j)\to 0

The inertia of the moduli stack of (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-polarized K3 surfaces at the point corresponding to (X¯,j)(\overline{X},j) is Γx/Wx​(Λ⟂)\Gamma_{x}/W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}) whereas the inertia of the stack [𝔻Λ:Γ][\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda}:\Gamma] at the point xx is certainly Γx\Gamma_{x}.

To resolve this problem, consider an open neighborhood Ux∋xU_{x}\ni x in 𝔻Λ\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda} preserved by the stabilizer Γx\Gamma_{x}. Take the quotient of UxU_{x} by Wx​(Λ⟂)W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}). Since Wx​(Λ⟂)⊂ΓxW_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp})\subset\Gamma_{x} is a normal subgroup, the quotient group Γx/Wx​(Λ⟂)=Aut⁡(X¯,j)\Gamma_{x}/W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp})={\rm Aut}(\overline{X},j) acts on the coarse space Ux/Wx​(Λ⟂)U_{x}/W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}).

Definition 5.3.

Define DM stack [𝔻Λ:WΓ][{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}:_{W}\Gamma] by gluing local charts of the form [Ux/Wx(Λ⟂):Γx/Wx(Λ⟂)][U_{x}/W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}):\Gamma_{x}/W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp})] ranging over all Γ\Gamma-orbits Γ⋅x⊂𝔻Λ\Gamma\cdot x\subset{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}.

Proposition 5.4.

[𝔻Λ:WΓ][{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}:_{W}\Gamma] is a smooth and separated DM stack.

Proof.

Since the quotient Ux/Wx​(Λ⟂)U_{x}/W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}) of a complex manifold by a reflection group is again a complex manifold, we see that [𝔻Λ:WΓ][{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}:_{W}\Gamma] is a smooth stack. It is separated because it factors the coarsening morphism [𝔻Λ:Γ]→[𝔻Λ:WΓ]→𝔻Λ/Γ[{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}\colon\Gamma]\to[{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}:_{W}\Gamma]\to{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}/\Gamma. ∎

Theorem 5.5.

For any hh contained in a small cone σ\sigma, the coarse moduli space FΛ,hF_{\Lambda,h} of (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-polarized K3 surfaces is isomorphic to 𝔻Λ/Γ\mathbb{D}_{\Lambda}/\Gamma, and the moduli stack ℱΛ,h{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h} is isomorphic to the separated DM stack [𝔻Λ:WΓ][{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}:_{W}\Gamma]. In particular, both are independent of hh.

Proof.

Given any family π:𝒳→S\pi\colon\mathcal{X}\to S of (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-quasipolarized K3 surfaces, there exists a simultaneous contraction of the positive roots in Λ⟂\Lambda^{\perp} on any fiber, by taking 𝒳→𝒳¯=ProjS⊕d≥0π∗ℒd,{\mathcal{X}}\to\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}=\Proj_{S}\oplus_{d\geq 0}\pi_{*}{\mathcal{L}}^{d}, for a relatively semiample element ℒ∈Pic⁡(𝒳/S){\mathcal{L}}\in{\rm Pic}({\mathcal{X}}/S) that represents an integral vector h′∈σh^{\prime}\in\sigma. The result is a family of (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-polarized K3 surfaces 𝒳¯→S\overline{\mathcal{X}}\to S.

Let C⊂SC\subset S be a curve, let 0∈C0\in C and C∗:=C∖0C^{*}:=C\setminus 0. As in Section 2, the family 𝒳¯\overline{\mathcal{X}} depends only on the classifying morphism C∗→[ℳΛ:Γ]C^{*}\to[\mathcal{M}_{\Lambda}:\Gamma] to the (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-quasipolarized moduli stack because we passed to the relatively ample model. We deduce from Corollary 4.22 that the coarse moduli space FΛ,hF_{\Lambda,h} is separated, and isomorphic to FΛ≃(ℳΛ/Γ)sep=𝔻Λ/ΓF_{\Lambda}\simeq({\mathcal{M}}_{\Lambda}/\Gamma)^{\rm sep}={\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}/\Gamma.

To identify the stack structure on ℱΛ,h{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h} as [𝔻Λ:WΓ][{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}:_{W}\Gamma], we first prove that the Kuranishi space of X¯{\overline{X}} is represented by the germ of (𝔻/Wx​(Λ⟂),x)({\mathbb{D}}/W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}),\,x). This deformation theory statement follows from unobstructedness ([BW74], cf. also [Nam01, Thm. 2.2]) together with [Bri71], which imply that the morphism of deformation functors Def⁡(X)→Def⁡(X¯){\rm Def}(X)\to{\rm Def}({\overline{X}}) given by simultaneous contraction to a configuration of ADE surface singularities (X¯,pi)∈X¯({\overline{X}},\,p_{i})\in{\overline{X}} is a Weyl group cover ∏iWpi=Wx​(Λ⟂)\prod_{i}W_{p_{i}}=W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}).

It follows that ℱΛ,h{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h} is locally identified with the stack

[𝔻Λ/Wx(Λ⟂):Γx/Wx(Λ⟂)][{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}/W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp}):\Gamma_{x}/W_{x}(\Lambda^{\perp})]

defining the :W:_{W}-quotient. In terms of automorphism groups: Any element of Aut⁡(X¯,j){\rm Aut}({\overline{X}},j) fixes j⁡(h)j(h) and thus descends to the ample model for hh, which is why the isotropy groups of ℱΛ,h{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h} are the same for any hh. ∎

Definition 5.6.

A generalized small cone τ\tau is the relative interior of a (locally) polyhedral face of some small cone σ\sigma, which contains a positive norm vector.

Note that every h∈Λ⊗ℝh\in\Lambda\otimes{\mathbb{R}}, h2>0h^{2}>0, lies in a unique generalized small cone τ\tau.

Remark 5.7.

Removing the condition in Definition 5.1 that hh lies in a small cone is subtle. In general, the linear system defined by some integral vector in the generalized small cone τ∋h\tau\ni h, will contract (−2)(-2)-curves whose classes do not lie in Λ⟂\Lambda^{\perp}. Thus, we do not always have an embedding of Λ\Lambda into Pic⁡(X¯){\rm Pic}({\overline{X}}), for the ample model X→X¯X\to{\overline{X}} with respect to hh.

Definition 5.8.

Let h∈Λ⊗ℝh\in\Lambda\otimes{\mathbb{R}}, h2>0h^{2}>0, be any positive norm vector. A family of (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-polarized K3 surfaces is a flat family f:𝒳¯→Sf\colon\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}\to S of ADE K3 surfaces, together with a simultaneous partial resolution 𝒳→S{\mathcal{X}}\to S to a family of (Λ,h′)(\Lambda,h^{\prime})-polarized K3 surfaces, where h′∈σh^{\prime}\in\sigma lies in a specified small cone σ\sigma containing hh in its closure. Here, by a partial resolution 𝒳→𝒳¯{\mathcal{X}}\to\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}, we mean a proper birational contraction over SS, which fiberwise over s∈Ss\in S sits between 𝒳¯s\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}_{s} and its minimal resolution.

Theorem 5.9.

Let τ∋h\tau\ni h be the unique generalized small cone containing a fixed vector h∈Λ⊗ℝh\in\Lambda\otimes{\mathbb{R}}, h2>0h^{2}>0. The stack of (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-polarized K3 surfaces, and the family 𝒳¯\overline{{\mathcal{X}}} over it, are independent of the choice of a small cone σ\sigma containing τ\tau in its closure. Furthermore, for all small cones σ\sigma containing τ\tau in their closure, 𝒳¯\overline{{\mathcal{X}}} admits a simultaneous crepant resolution to a family of (Λ,σ)(\Lambda,\sigma)-polarized K3 surfaces.

Proof.

Let h′∈σh^{\prime}\in\sigma be an element of the chosen small cone σ\sigma involved in Definition 5.8, of the moduli stack of (Λ,h)(\Lambda,h)-polarized K3 surfaces.

We claim there is an isomorphism of functors ℱΛ,h→ℱΛ,h′{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h}\to{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h^{\prime}}. On the one hand, by definition, the universal family over the former stack is endowed with a simultaneous partial resolution to a family of (Λ,h′)(\Lambda,h^{\prime})-polarized K3 surfaces, giving the forward map. Conversely, there is an inverse map ℱΛ,h′→ℱΛ,h{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h^{\prime}}\to{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h} by passing to the ample model for some integral vector in the generalized small cone τ∋h\tau\ni h, which is relatively semiample on any family of (Λ,h′)(\Lambda,h^{\prime})-polarized K3 surfaces.

By Theorem 5.5, for two small cones σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} containing τ\tau in their closure, the moduli stacks ℱΛ,σ1{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,\sigma_{1}} and ℱΛ,σ2{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,\sigma_{2}} are naturally isomorphic. Next, the hh-ample models 𝒳¯1\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}_{1} and 𝒳¯2\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}_{2} of the universal families 𝒳σ1→ℱΛ,σ1{\mathcal{X}}_{\sigma_{1}}\to{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,\sigma_{1}} and 𝒳σ2→ℱΛ,σ2{\mathcal{X}}_{\sigma_{2}}\to{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,\sigma_{2}} for σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} are isomorphic, since hh is relatively ample on these contractions. Thus the universal family 𝒳¯1≃𝒳¯2≃𝒳¯\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}_{1}\simeq\overline{{\mathcal{X}}}_{2}\simeq\overline{{\mathcal{X}}} is independent of the choice of σ\sigma. ∎

Corollary 5.10.

With respect to Definition 5.8, the statement of Theorem 5.5 holds for any h∈Λ⊗ℝh\in\Lambda\otimes{\mathbb{R}}, h2>0h^{2}>0.

Remark 5.11.

The map ℱΛ,hq→ℱΛ,h{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm q}_{\Lambda,h}\to{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h} is modeled on the following simple example.

Let 𝔸t1∪𝔸t1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t}\cup{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t} be a “line with doubled origin”, a non-separated scheme obtained by gluing two affine lines 𝔸t1=Spec⁡ℂ⁡[t]{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t}=\Spec{\mathbb{C}}[t] along 𝔸1∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus 0, and let 𝔸t21=Spec⁡ℂ⁡[t2]{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t^{2}}=\Spec{\mathbb{C}}[t^{2}]. Over a transverse arc slicing the Heegner divisor {x∈𝔻Λ:β⋅x=0}\{x\in{\mathbb{D}}_{\Lambda}\,:\,\beta\cdot x=0\}, β∈Λ⟂\beta\in\Lambda^{\perp}, the stack ℱΛ,hq{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm q}_{\Lambda,h} is locally modeled on (𝔸t1∪𝔸t1)/W({\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t}\cup{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t})/W, W=S2=⟨rβ⟩W=S_{2}=\langle r_{\beta}\rangle, acting on each 𝔸t1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t} by t→−tt\to-t and interchanging the two origins. So the action of WW is free. This quotient is a non-separated algebraic space (it would be a non-separated stack if we divided by a bigger group Γ⊃W\Gamma\supset W). The stack ℱΛ,h{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h} in this case is modeled on the scheme 𝔸t21{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t^{2}} and the map ℱΛ,hq→ℱΛ,h{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm q}_{\Lambda,h}\to{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h} is modeled on

(𝔸t1∪𝔸t1)/S2→𝔸t1/S2=𝔸t21.({\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t}\cup{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t})/S_{2}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t}/S_{2}={\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t^{2}}.

As we see, the morphism ℱΛ,hq→ℱΛ,h{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h}^{\rm q}\to{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h} is a ramified WtW_{t}-cover for all t∈𝔸t1t\in{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{t}.

Suppose that a non-separated DM stack ℱ{\mathcal{F}} admits charts [U:G][U:G], for which the union of charts [Usep:G][U^{\rm sep}:G] is a separated DM stack ℱsep{\mathcal{F}}^{\rm sep}. The stack ℱΛ,hq{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h}^{\rm q} satisfies this condition, and with respect to this notion of separated quotient, [AE23, Thm. 2.11] is false, i.e. (ℱΛ,hq)sep≄ℱΛ,h({\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h}^{\rm q})^{\rm sep}\not\simeq{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h}. Though [AE23, Rem. 2.12] describes the correct stack structure on ℱΛ,h{\mathcal{F}}_{\Lambda,h} as in Definition 5.3 and Theorem 5.5.

It is unclear what is the most general set-up in which one has the separated “:W:_{W}-quotient” that appears in Theorem 5.5. We expect that roughly, one needs a split exact sequence as in (1)—that is, a normal subgroup of the relevant group of Hodge isometries, which acts on the different birational models which appear as quasipolarized fillings of punctured families.

For instance, the results in this paper should extend to moduli of polarized primitive symplectic varieties (X¯,L¯)({\overline{X}},{\overline{L}}), which play the role of ADE K3 surfaces, and a ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-factorial terminalization X→X¯X\to{\overline{X}}, which plays the role of the quasipolarized minimal resolution, see [BL22] and [LMP24, Thm. 3.7].

In this regard, we note some existing literature about the moduli spaces of smooth irreducible holomorphic symplectic manifolds: [Cam16, Cam18, Jou16].
